In Minnesota you do need a government issued photo ID to register to vote. You also need some other item with your name and address on it to verify your eligible to vote in that location. It can be a utility bill, banking or credit card statement etc. And it needs to be postmarked within 30 days of the election.

You can register in advance, or do same day registration at the polling place.

The system will know if you have already voted in a different city or county.

This is where the system breaks down, but not as badly as some may think.

If you are already registered and in the system, you do not need to present your ID at the polls. You only need to say who you are and to verify your home address. You will then be presented with a voters oath form that you must sign. You are signing this oath under penalty of law, which states that this is you, and this is your home residence.

It is possible for someone to go to the polls and claim to be you, and vote in your name.

And if you try to vote, the system won’t let you. In my years of being an election judge, I have only seen this happen once.

Logistically that seems to be a pretty tall order, and not likely for any group to accomplish.

Every step of the voting management process is conducted with one election judge from each party to ensure impartiality in counting out ballots. And each must sign their names validating their counts. There is multiple reporting procedures to ensure mistakes don’t happen. And in the case a mistake does happen, everything is reported in an incident log. These logs can be viewed by request from your city clerk. The process is transparent, but you do need to ask to view any aspect of the process and it will be provided to you.

I should add that the ballot tabulators are also not connected to the internet, so they cannot be remotely hacked.

I would suggest that if anyone is concerned about the sanctity of your vote, and would like to find out how the system works, step up and volunteer to be an eclectic judge. You are paid for your time for both training sessions and for the time spent at the polls as a judge.

To make the system better, we need honest election judges to be witness to the process to ensure cheating is not possible.
